voce: ZwZ2-9B lifts overall accuracy from 51.63 % to 56.59 % across 25 benchmarks. It does this without any extra supervised fine-tuning.

ZwZ2-9B is a 9.4 billion-parameter model built on the Qwen3.5-9B backbone. The model is trained on whole images, not cropped patches, and can handle a context window of 256 K tokens. It is released by InclusionAI and available for free on Hugging Face. The model card lists the size, the base model, and the training approach, giving hobbyists a clear picture of what they are downloading.

The core novelty is the EvidenceConnect pipeline. It builds verified questions that span three to seven related image regions, using privileged zoomed views just for data construction. Answers are checked through cross-model agreement and drop-one-region tests, then turned into four-option tasks. Training uses the GRPO method and skips any additional supervised fine-tuning stage, keeping the process simple and efficient.

According to the model card, ZwZ2-9B was evaluated on twenty-five benchmarks covering fine-grained perception, spatial reasoning, long-context understanding, multimodal agents, and general visual reasoning. Across all of them the model improves over its Qwen3.5-9B base, raising the average accuracy from 51.63 % to 56.59 %, a gain of 4.96 points. The improvement is consistent on every benchmark, showing the method’s broad impact.

The model’s strengths lie in its enhanced ability to connect visual evidence across regions, which translates into better fine-grained perception and stronger spatial and long-context reasoning. However, the model card warns that it can still hallucinate details, misread text, and make counting or spatial errors. Performance also depends on image resolution, context length, and prompt format, so careful prompt engineering helps mitigate these limits.

ZwZ2-9B is a good fit for hobbyists who run AI models at home and need visual reasoning capabilities without paying for an API. The model can run on a modest RTX 4060, making it accessible to many desktop setups. If you want a free, open-weight model that improves visual understanding over a strong base, ZwZ2-9B is worth a try.

What do you need to run it at home? At 4-bit it takes about 8 gigabytes of memory. The smallest home machine that holds it fully is an RTX 40 60. On an RTX 30 60 12 GB with 32 gigabytes of RAM it writes about 45 tokens per second. On an RTX 40 90 with 64 gigabytes of RAM it writes about 116 tokens per second.

There is no free API for it yet. The weights are open: you can download them from Hugging Face, under the license written in its model card. Arena has not ranked it yet: we add the score as soon as the votes arrive.
